entries.title: Mbappe apologizes as Chinese sponsors drop him and TV broadcasts are halted over Mao dictator remark
entries.summary: French soccer star Kylian Mbappe has apologized after apparently referring to Mao Zedong as a dictator. Chinese sponsors have dropped him, while state television has suspended Spanish league broadcasts.
entries.content:
October 27, 2026

French soccer star Kylian Mbappe has apologized after apparently referring to Mao Zedong as a dictator. Chinese sponsors have dropped him, while state television has suspended Spanish league broadcasts.

France striker Kylian Mbappe apologized after apparently referring to China's founding leader Mao Zedong as a dictator in a video that circulated online.

The controversy prompted three major Chinese companies to sever sponsorship ties with the Real Madrid forward, while Chinese state television suspended broadcasts of Spain's La Liga.

What did Mbappe say about Mao?

The controversy began when a video circulated showing Mbappe discussing his favorite internet meme featuring himself.

In the clip, apparently filmed ahead of an appearance on the French online talk show The Bridge, Mbappe referred to an image depicting his face superimposed on the body of "some guy ... I think he's a Chinese dictator."

The image appeared to depict Mao Zedong, who founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled until his death in 1976. Jokes about country’s former leader and descriptions of him as a dictator remain taboo.

Mbappe has previously been depicted as authoritarian leaders in online memes mocking his perceived influence over teammates the suggestions that he has the power to influence club decisions.

Mbappe has been nicknamed "the dictator" in the European press.

How did Mbappe apologize?

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappe said in a statement.

"I apologize to everyone my words have upset. This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry."

Chinese sponsors cut ties with Mbappe

Chinese beverage company Dongpeng, dairy producer Mengniu and cheesemaker Milkground announced they were ending their partnerships with the French international.

In similarly worded statements, each said that they oppose "any words and actions that hurt national sentiment."

China Media Group, which oversees state broadcaster CCTV, also suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches and removed advertisements featuring Mbappe.

La Liga apologized for the controversy, saying Mbappe's comments were made in a personal capacity and did not represent the Spanish league.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV subsequently said it would consider Mbappe's apology but would also judge his future actions.

In response to a question about the controversy, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that "words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."

Why is Mao such a sensitive subject in China?

Mao remains a revered figure in China, where public criticism of the former Communist leader is politically sensitive.

His rule was also marked by disastrous political campaigns, including the Great Leap Forward, which contributed to a famine that killed tens of millions of people.

The ruling Communist Party acknowledges some of his mistakes but maintains that his achievements outweighed them, making criticism of his legacy politically sensitive.

Edited by: Alex Berry

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: Myanmar: Is the US undermining the EU's diplomatic blockade?
entries.summary: With the US reopening talks with Myanmar's military-backed government, and several Southeast Asian countries restarting diplomatic contacts, the EU is facing uncomfortable questions about its own boycott of the junta.
entries.content:
Myanmar

Myanmar: Is the US undermining the EU's diplomatic blockade?

October 27, 2026

With the US reopening talks with Myanmar's military-backed government, and several Southeast Asian countries restarting diplomatic contacts, the EU is facing uncomfortable questions about its own boycott of the junta.

The US government has begun a quiet reproachment with Myanmar's military-backed government, holding two rounds of talks since September with State Department representative Michael Vance. American diplomats reportedly meet Myanmar officials in Naypyitaw and then in Tokyo earlier this month.

Washington wants to tackle online scam centers, secure the release of imprisoned American businessman Adam Castillo, and potentially gain access to Myanmar's rare-earth resources. The market for the valuable minerals is currently controlled by the US rival China.

Meanwhile, Southeast Asian governments are also increasingly questioning their policy of isolating Myanmar's military leadership. Multiple countries have already renewed direct diplomatic contacts.

The EU, however, continues to reject the legitimacy of the military junta in the war-torn country. The European bloc has also remained unmoved by the 2025/2026 election, which ended with military chief Min Aung Hlaing becoming the president. The military retains control over the political system.

EU's sanctions still in force

The EU responded to Myanmar's February 2021 military coup by suspending direct financial assistance to the government, imposing targeted sanctions and sharply reducing diplomatic engagement with the military authorities.

Its sanctions currently cover 105 individuals and 22 entities connected to the military. In April, the EU extended these measures for another 12 months.

At the same time, Brussels is providing humanitarian assistance to displaced communities and Rohingya refugees and is supporting civil society organizations.

The EU also stopped short of withdrawing Myanmar's preferential trade access because of concerns about the consequences for workers, particularly the mostly young women employed in the country's garment industry. Last year, bilateral goods trade was worth about €4 billion ($4.46 billion), up from €3.4 billion in 2019.

Brussels supports ASEAN's peace deal

The civil war triggered by the 2021 coup has killed an estimated 100,000 people. Rebel groups still control or contest large swathes of Myanmar, and over 4 million people have been internally displaced, according to UN data.

The EU "continues to uphold its policy of non-recognition of the current military regime," in view of "the ongoing violence and the attack against its own population," an EU spokesman told DW.

At the same time, the bloc "is closely monitoring developments in the discussions and positions of the United States, Japan, ASEAN countries and other major actors with representatives of Myanmar's military regime."

"It also supports ASEAN efforts, in particular the Five-Point Consensus, which has yet to be fully implemented," the spokesperson added, referring to the peace deal proposed by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2021.

Myanmar diplomats reach out to European partners

In the aftermath of the coup, ASEAN took the unprecedented decision to exclude Myanmar's military leaders from its highest-level meetings after the junta failed to implement the regional peace plan.

However, ASEAN's position is showing signs of change. Some member states, most notably Myanmar's neighbor Thailand, signal growing frustration with the lack of progress towards ending Myanmar's civil war.

Last week, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow welcomed Washington's renewed engagement and suggested that ASEAN members would hold substantive discussions about Myanmar's future at their summit in Manila next month.

Myanmar's authorities are also seeking to break their diplomatic isolation. In September, Myanmar's leader Hlaing gave an interview to Time magazine, his first with a major Western publication since the coup, as part of an apparent effort to rebuild relations with Western governments.

On October 22, Burma Campaign UK, a London-based human rights organization, accused the British government of making a "significant shift in approach" after the British Foreign Office hosted Win Zeyar Tun, the charge d'affaires of Myanmar's military-controlled embassy in London, at an ASEAN diplomatic gathering days earlier.

According to an article published by Intelligence Online this month, the regime's charge d'affaires in Brussels, Khin Thidar Ay, has also sought contacts with European politicians, including Czech MEP Ondrej Dostal, a member of the European Parliament's delegation for Southeast Asia.

EU's isolation 'has achieved relatively little'

Kristina Kironska, of Palacky University Olomouc in the Czech Republic and an expert on the EU's policy on Myanmar, told DW that the EU has little reason to follow Washington's apparent shift towards engagement with the Myanmar junta.

The US strategy "appears to be pursuing specific interests" such as rare earth mining and cybercrime, she said.

However, the most important rare earth mining operations are no longer controlled by the military, but by rebels such as the Kachin Independence Organization in Kachin State. "It remains to be seen what the US can achieve through negotiations with the junta," she said.

The EU has long positioned itself as a defender of democracy and human rights in Myanmar, "so abandoning this now because the US is exploring a new, perhaps more transactional approach would undermine the EU's credibility," Kironska added.

"At the same time, isolation has achieved relatively little. The question is therefore not whether the EU should engage, but rather with whom and under what conditions."

Balancing act between Myanmar's rebels and junta

The EU is forced to consider risks to its own influence. If Washington, ASEAN governments and other regional powers increase their engagement with Myanmar's authorities, the EU risks becoming increasingly marginal in discussions about the country's political future.

Yet greater engagement with the military could undermine Brussels' relations with Myanmar's democratic opposition and ethnic resistance organizations, many of which control substantial territory.

"The key question for Brussels is whether it can remain a credible defender of democratic change while ensuring that it still has a meaningful voice in the negotiations that will determine Myanmar's future," Sabe Soe, director of the NGO Burma Centre Prague, told DW.

One possibility is for Brussels to maintain its sanctions against military leaders and their businesses while expanding diplomacy through ASEAN, the UN and other regional partners. The EU could also tie any easing of restrictions to humanitarian access, improvements in political freedoms and progress towards peace.

Soe also suggested that the EU could pursue economic engagement in areas administered by revolutionary and ethnic resistance forces, offering an alternative to engagement centred on the military authorities in Naypyidaw.

This approach would allow the EU to remain involved in Myanmar's future without necessarily recognizing its military-backed government, she said.

For now, Brussels seems to have little appetite for a fundamental policy rethink. But this could change as more governments reopen their doors to Myanmar's generals.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Turnout at Israel's election has reached a record high at the halfway stage
entries.summary: Almost 45% of the electorate had voted by 2 p.m., the highest share since such records began in 1973. The highly anticipated vote is expected to be a close-fought contest, and perhaps even a stalemate.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel election: Turnout at record levels at halfway stage

Published October 27, 2026last updated October 27, 2026

Almost 45% of the electorate had voted by 2 p.m., the highest share since such records began in 1973. The highly anticipated vote is expected to be a close-fought contest, and perhaps even a stalemate.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Israelis voting to elect Knesset
  • Israel election committee reports highest voter turnout on record as of 2 p.m., halfway through the voting day
  • Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, faces a staunch challenge to his grip on power
  • His chief rival is former military chief Gadi Eisenkot
  • Eisenkot's Yashar party has polled higher than Netanyahu's Likud party

Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and its aftermath:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section WATCH: Could Arab voters hold the key in Israel’s election?

WATCH: Could Arab voters hold the key in Israel’s election?

Arab voters could play a decisive role in Israel's election. With neither Benjamin Netanyahu nor Gadi Eisenkot expected to win a Knesset majority, Arab parties could become key to forming the next government.

Activists worked to boost voter turnout, especially among young voters.

Skip next section Netanyahu emphasizes Arab turnout in appeals to his own voters

Netanyahu emphasizes Arab turnout in appeals to his own voters

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu continued issuing appeals to supporters to go out and vote online as the day progressed. 

One common theme was apparent in almost all of the posts: warnings about high turnout in Arab and to a lesser extent left-leaning communities.

"We're at war for our home," one of Netanyahu's posts read, using a phrase that appeared repeatedly in his messaging. "Muslim Brotherhood supporters are raiding the polling stations and stealing the elections. Go out and vote, recover it!!"

In another post he showed an image claiming to show a long line of voters queueing in Rahat, with a crowd of women wearing niqab coverings prominently visible at the front of the queue, suggesting that they were Muslim Palestinian voters.

Sami Abou Shahadeh, the leader of the Balad party, which is part of the alliance known as the Joint List, in turn called on his supporters to vote before the deadline expired, also highlighting similar appeals to voters from the leader of the far-right Jewish Power party, Itamar Ben-Gvir.

"There is one response to the incitement by Ben-Gvir and Netanyahu against the Arab citizens that has been going on all day: go out and vote for the Joint List!" he wrote.

Skip next section President of German-Israeli Society, Volker Beck, says a change would be 'good for Israel'

President of German-Israeli Society, Volker Beck, says a change would be 'good for Israel'

The president of the German-Israeli Society, Green party politician Volker Beck, said in a TV interview on election day that he believed a change in leadership might be in Israel's interests.

"It would be good for Israel, if it were to come to a change, because I believe that [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu has squandered a great deal of trust in recent years, both in foreign and domestic policy," Beck said in an interview broadcast on sister channels RTL and ntv.

Beck, a Bundestag lawmaker for more than two decades with the Greens who was perhaps best known as a politician as a campaigner for LGBT rights and advocate of an uncompromising Israeli foreign policy, is not typically associated with stern criticism of Netanyahu or his government. 

"Although he has also done some things right and has done some necessary things, a change is really needed" to allow Israel to recoup support among the international community, Beck said, as Netanyahu becomes an increasingly polarizing figure on the world stage.

He also criticized domestic efforts by the Likud-led government to reform the legal system and its influence over politics, saying this would "fundamentally change Israel's character, and should be stopped."

Beck said he hoped that a functioning majority would emerge from the vote, but acknowledged that pollsters anticipated a stalemate. In that scenario, he said, he would personally favor a national unity government incorporating all the major players.

But at present he thought the "divide between the two camps is so deep, that it really would be a bit of a masterstroke to be able to bring them together." He made a similar comment online, saying such a unity govermment "would be good" but was "not very likely."

Skip next section Likud says online that it has requested an extension of voting hours

Likud says online that it has requested an extension of voting hours

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party wrote on the Telegram social media channel that it has submitted a request for polling stations to stay open later. 

"Likud: We have submitted a request to extend the voting hours!" the post said.

It offered no further details, for instance, how long an extension it was seeking or whether it was to be nationwide or at individual polling stations.

The Ultra-Orthodox Shas party also joined the petition, according to the Times of Israel, saying: "The parties are trying to prevent a situation in which citizens waiting in line won’t be able to vote."

The main opposition Yashar party rejected the extension, saying: "No exceptional incident has occurred that would justify granting this request, which is intended to lay the groundwork for allegations challenging the integrity of the election, continuing the lies Netanyahu has been spreading since this morning."

Politicians of all stripes have been trying hard to mobilize voters for what's expected to be a tight race. Turnout has also been high so far, with long lines at some polling stations as a result of this.

Voting was already set to continue quite late into the night, with polling stations scheduled to close at 10 p.m. local time. Voters who are in line at polling stations at closing time will still be allowed to vote.

Skip next section Who are Israel's first-time voters projected to support?

Who are Israel's first-time voters projected to support?

Polls show Israel's many young voters are more likely to vote for far-right parties, particularly Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party.

An opinion poll by Agam Labs at Jerusalem's Hebrew University predicts that supporters of Otzma Yehudit are younger than the average Israeli voter, with as many as a third voting for the first time.

Over 500,000 Israelis have reached voting age since the 2022 election. Of those voters, three in every four define themselves as right or center-right, according to a recent poll for Channel 12. The poll did not survey Palestinian citizens of Israel.

First-time voters were teenagers when Ben-Gvir joined Netanyahu's incumbent government in 2022, making up Israel's most far-right government to date.

A year later, they witnessed the Hamas-led October 7 terror attack which killed 1,200 Israelis, mostly civilians, and saw some 251 others taken hostage and brought to Gaza. The attack triggered a 2-year war on the Palestinian enclave that resulted in tens of thousands of Palestinians killed and intensified settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. Hamas is designated as a terrorist group by several countries.

Previously, Otzma Yehudit's support was concentrated primarily among settlers in the occupied West Bank.

Skip next section WATCH — Author, politician Avraham Burg on why a Palestinian peace process barely featured in the campaign

WATCH — Author, politician Avraham Burg on why a Palestinian peace process barely featured in the campaign

While security remained the dominant issue for Israeli voters, one topic was largely absent from the election campaign: a peace process with the Palestinians.

After years of conflict and failed negotiations, that debate has been pushed to the political margins.

Has Israeli society abandoned the idea of coexistence?

Avraham Burg, an Israeli writer and former Speaker of the Israeli Parliament, shares his insights with DW.

Skip next section Turnout reaches highest level on record at halfway point

Turnout reaches highest level on record at halfway point

Turnout in Israel's election keeps rising. It reached a record 44.9% by 2 p.m. (1200 UTC), the Central Elections Commission said.

Some 3.29 million Israelis had cast their ballots by that point, commission head Dean Livne said.

It was the highest turnout recorded at that hour since the commission began collecting comparable statistics in 1973.

Skip next section Eisenkot promises 'change' after casting his vote

Eisenkot promises 'change' after casting his vote

Gadi Eisenkot, the main challenger to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, urged voters on Tuesday to oust what he called the "worst government" in Israel's history and promised a more responsible style of leadership.

"There is a wind of change blowing in Israel, and this change will come into effect tonight at 10 p.m.," at which point polls close, he said after casting his own vote at a polling station in Holon, just south of Tel-Aviv.

"We will not lead Israel through division and scaremongering, but through unity and true love," he said. "We will win!"

Ahead of election day, Israeli pollsters had predicted a close race between Netanyahu's right-wing conservatives and Eisenkot's opposition bloc, with neither expected to win an outright majority.

"I call on all citizens of Israel to vote, not to buckle under the heat or the disruptions, to stick to the mission," said Eisenkot. "To replace tonight the worst government since the state was established."

Skip next section WATCH: How Israel's PM Netanyahu holds on to power

WATCH: How Israel's PM Netanyahu holds on to power

Three years after the Hamas-led October 7 attacks exposed major flaws in Israeli security, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains the dominant figure in Israel's political landscape. DW examines how many Israeli voters judge him more on his response to the crisis than on the failures that preceded it.

Experts point to security concerns, fear, Israel's conflicts on multiple fronts, and the absence of a clear challenger as key factors behind Netanyahu's resilience. The report also explores why international criticism can strengthen his support ahead of Israel's upcoming Knesset election.

Skip next section Netanyahu casts ballot, while accusing Arab-Israeli parties of fraud

Netanyahu casts ballot, while accusing Arab-Israeli parties of fraud

Israel's Central Elections Committee said on Tuesday that "there are currently no indications of systematic tampering with ballot slips" after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Arab-Israeli parties of "trying to steal the election."

Netanyahu made the allegation after casting his own ballot in Jerusalem while urging voters to choose his Likud party.

"We know what is at stake ... We cannot leave this battle here in the hands of the left and the Arab parties that want to bring an end to the Jewish state," he said.

Netanyahu has used Arab-Israeli parties throughout the election to stoke fears of a Palestinian state and mobilize voters for Likud.

"So no barbecues, don't go to the beach — go to the polling station and vote Likud."

Netanyahu had said that three senior officials from the opposition Ra'am party, which has an Arab Muslim voter base, had been arrested in southern Israel with envelopes full of cash.

The acting director general of the Central Elections Committee, Dean Livne, referred to the "unusual" incident with the envelopes in a press conference Tuesday morning but said that "police, even before people arrived at the polling stations, caught individuals who tried to bribe voters."

He said the unidentified suspects were not actually at polling stations and were caught near their homes, adding the matter was under investigation.

"There are no similar incidents of this kind across the country," he concluded. "This was a localized case."

Opposition parties, including that of Netanyahu's main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, have also complained that ballot papers were being defaced and stolen at polling stations.

Skip next section Early Israel election turnout highest in decades

Early Israel election turnout highest in decades

Voter turnout in the first three hours of the Israeli general election was the highest in decades, Israel's Central Elections Committee said on Tuesday.

According to the committee, nationwide turnout by mid-morning was already at 16.68%, the highest at this stage of the vote since 1981 and up from 15.9% at the same time in the 2022 election.

"By 10 a.m., more than 1,200,000 Israelis had voted," said the committee's acting director general, Dean Livne.

Total voter turnout in Israeli general elections approached 80% the 1990s but hasn't been higher than 72.3% since the turn of the century. Turnout at the last general election in 2022 was 70.6%.

Turnout among Arab Israelis is expected to be particularly important given the role Arab parties could play as potential kingmakers in coalition talks.

"Our vote will change the government," predicted Mansour Abbas, head of the Islamist Ra'am party as he cast his vote, adding that he hoped turnout would surpass 70% in Arab communities.

Arabs in Israel make up about 18% of the electorate, and pre-election surveys have suggested a sharp increase in voter participation.

Data from the Midgam Research Institute cited by the Qatar-owned The New Arab indicates that turnout within the Arab community could rise to between 62% and 63%, up from approximately 53% in previous elections. The National, based in the United Arab Emirates, said its sources were predicting an "astronomical" Arab turnout.

Skip next section How does Israel's election work?

How does Israel's election work?

Who is eligible to vote?

Around 7.3 million Israelis (including around 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel) are eligible to vote on Tuesday.

More than 640,000 young Israelis will be eligible to vote in a general election for the first time.

Around 3.1 million Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank do not have the right to vote in Israeli elections, but 500,000 illegal settlers in those territories do.

A further 350,000 Palestinians live in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem and also cannot vote, whereas around 230,000 Israelis living there can.

The US-based non-profit America-Israel Democracy Coalition (AID Coalition) has organized a "Fly&Vote" initiative, with as many as 67,000 voters returning to Israel to participate in the election, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data.

The coalition said half are coming from the US, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Israel does not have postal voting.

How does the voting system work?

Israel is a parliamentary democracy and voters elect a legislature rather than choosing their prime minister directly. Voters choose a party "list."

Israel uses a proportional representation system under which 120 parliamentary seats are distributed roughly in proportion to a party's share of the vote.

To enter parliament (known as the Knesset), parties must receive at least 3.25% of valid votes, which is equivalent to roughly four seats.

The party which can command a majority of at least 61 seats is called upon to form a government. No single party has ever won an outright majority, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions. Polls suggest this year will be no different.

Unlike many other democracies around the world, Israel is not divided up into geographic electoral districts.

Rather than electing individual lawmakers to represent local areas, voters in Tel Aviv, Jerusalem and Haifa all choose from the same party lists in one, single, nationwide constituency.

When polling stations close at 10 p.m. local time (9 p.m. CET), broadcasters will publish their first exit polls, offering an initial indication of the results. Official results are scheduled to be published on November 4.

Skip next section Arab-Israeli parties: Potential kingmakers in Israel's future ruling coalition?

Arab-Israeli parties: Potential kingmakers in Israel's future ruling coalition?

While the main competition for the largest number of seats is between Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, the Arab parties are projected to play a key role in determining Israel's next ruling coalition.

For a party or coalition to rule, it needs to secure 61 seats in the Knesset.

As per a recent Channel 12 poll, Eisenkot's bloc is hovering around 55 seats, while Netanyahu's bloc is trailing behind with some 51 seats. This means that either bloc would need to form coalitions in order to rule, should the election results come out similar to the polls.

The most likely parties to tip the scales are the Joint List (projected to win around 9 seats) and the Ra'am (projected to win around 5 seats). The Arab minority, who are Palestinian by heritage but Israeli by nationality, make up around a fifth of Israel's eligible voters. Polls suggest a higher turnout rate for the Arab voters than seen in previous elections.

Netanyahu's Likud and Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudi parties attempted last month to ban the Joint List and Ra'am from running in the race, but Israel's Supreme Court reversed the parties' disqualification earlier in October.

Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu have ruled out an alliance with the Arab parties. But analysts suggest such stances are not set in stone and can shift amid coalition talks, a move Netanyahu himself has resorted to in the past.

Skip next section Gadi Eisenkot: Who is Netanyahu's main opponent?

Gadi Eisenkot: Who is Netanyahu's main opponent?

The Israeli general election is considered by many to be a verdict on the country's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

But who is the opposition, and what do they stand for?

The main opposition force is a so-called "change bloc," a mixed group of center-right and some left-wing parties led by the newly formed Yashar (honesty) party and its leader Gadi Eisenkot.

A relative political newcomer, Eisenkot is the son of Moroccan immigrants who rose to become the chief of the staff of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) between 2015 and 2019.

Eisenkot has positioned himself squarely in opposition to Netanyahu in terms of his personality — an unpolished man of the people in contrast to the highly stylized and controlling prime minister.

Campaigning on accountability, political reform, and national unity, Eisenkot has sharply criticized Netanyahu's leadership before and after the October 7 Hamas attacks.

But his politics don't differ massively and, although he has emphasized equal rights for all Israeli citizens, he has been ambiguous on the idea of a two-state solution since October 7.

While backing Israel's military operations, he argues the government lacks a clear strategy and has called for an independent inquiry into the failures surrounding the attacks. His military record and the death of his son in the Gaza war have strengthened his standing among many voters

The parties in Eisenkot's bloc all have ideological differences but are united by their goal of removing Netanyahu from power.

Skip next section Polls open in Israel election

Polls open in Israel election

Voting began in Israel at 7 a.m. local time (6 a.m. CET) on Tuesday in the first general election since the deadly Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, and the devastating war in Gaza unleashed by Israel in response.

Some 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote, with polls showing a bloc led by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving premier, neck and neck with Gadi Eisenkot's centrist opposition alliance.

Most polling stations will close at 10 p.m. local time (8 p.m. UTC).

entries.title: Harry Kane: Ballon d’Or for Bayern Munich striker
entries.summary: Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has won football's most prestigious individual prize, beating Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.
entries.content:
October 27, 2026

Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has won football's most prestigious individual prize, beating Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.

To most Bayern Munich fans under the age of 40, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge was the club CEO who regularly spoke his mind. Fans with longer memories, or a better grasp of Bavarian football history, recall Rummenigge as one of the club's all-time great players. He was also the last Bayern man to win the Ballon d'Or — in 1981. The last Bundesliga player to win was Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Sammer, in 1996.

That long drought ended on Monday, with Harry Kane, born 12 years after Rummenigge's win, picking up the 2026 trophy at a ceremony held, as a one-off, in his native London.

"I am almost speechless. Being here in London has made it extra special,” he said on stage.

Not many people would have thought it, and maybe even I wouldn't have thought I'd be this far," Kane later told British sports streaming plaftorm DAZN.

Lamine Yamal, the prodigious Barcelona and Spain forward who won the Euros at 16, finished third. At the end of the 2025-26 season, on which the award is judged, Yamal won the World Cup with Spain as well as the La Liga title. Kylian Mbappe came in second.

Kane's career not just measured in numbers

Kane's 73 goals for club and country last season made for a strong case, and the Bundesliga's most expensive signing of all time has already racked up 156 goals in 159 games for the serial German champions. But it's not just the numbers that tell the story, according to his club coach.

"People in England saw him as a goalscorer during his time playing there," Vincent Kompany said of Kane last season. "We've seen other qualities too, such as his footballing intelligence. We can appreciate that now — it was perhaps somewhat underestimated in England. He's like a fine wine that improves with age. I also enjoy that aspect of his game."

Kane continues to improve at 33, a point when many footballers start to regress. Though he is helped by being more reliant on guile and technique than pace, Kane's professionalism is key to staying at the top, according to his Bayern teammate Serge Gnabry.

"He always has the right attitude, always leads the way and sets the tone," Gnabry said ahead of Bayern's 2-2 draw in the Champions League against Arsenal last week. "He never strays from his path, helps the team with his performance and is a top-tier player."

Kane scored a penalty in that match and provided a sensational pass from which Alphonso Davies scored Bayern's opener, another reminder of his all-round game. "The pass was one of my best ones," Kane said after the match. "I knew Phonzy [Davies] would be able to get there with his speed. Whatever I can do to help the team, I'll do. At the moment, it seems to be with assists more than goals."

Kane's 'greatest strength'

That attitude has been with Kane from the start. His first-ever coach, Dave Bricknell, from Ridgeway Rovers, an amateur club in northeast London, told DW after Kane joined Bayern from Spurs in 2023: "Harry's mentality is his greatest strength. He doesn't let anything worry him. If he misses a chance, he doesn't care — he will go and score from another chance."

His England coach, Thomas Tuchel, has also emphasized Kane's leadership. "He is the first one to push everyone, and that is his mindset, and he became a very, very hardworking forward on top of his finishing skills, Tuchel said in September as Kane extended his England goal-scoring record against the Czech Republic. "He is a complete package."

There are detractors who point to perceived "stat-padding," or scoring against inferior opponents in international qualifiers and in the Bundesliga, where there are fewer elite teams and a lot less money, than in England. Though Kane's ratio of 213 goals in 320 games in the Premier League is a little off his Bundesliga stats, it bears comparison with any other player in the history of the league.

Kane winning the award is also a boost in profile for the Bundesliga, which has been unable to keep pace, both commercially and on the pitch, with other top European leagues of late, particularly the Premier League and La Liga.

Winning it in a league outside of England or Spain perhaps makes Kane's feat even greater. Other than Ousmane Dembele, who won it last year after Paris Saint-Germain's Champions League win, and Lionel Messi, a serial Ballon d'Or winner, the last player to take the Ballon d'Or for a season played outside England or Spain was was Kaka at AC Milan in 2007, when Italy's Serie A was considered a stronger league.

Kane's career hasn't been straightforward, something he admitted in his speech. After signing his first senior contract with Spurs in July 2010, he was sent out on various loans to lower league sides between 2011-2013 without ever making a huge impression.

"My journey wasn't straightforward. I wasn't the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs, I had a lot of loan moves, I had to fight my way to be the very best right now, and I hope that can give you determination as well," Kane said in his speech.

Domestic trophies won but international success eludes

For former teammate Jermain Defoe, who also coached Kane at Spurs, those experiences were formative.

"You have to show a resilience. It's not easy when you go out on loan, it can feel like you're being rejected by the club that you are at, which isn't the case," he told DW in 2023, before adding that Kane's ability was always clear.

"When he joined up with the [Tottenham] first team, you could see the potential," Defoe said. "He was always a good finisher, always hit the ball clean. … With Harry you already knew, he had that natural instinct and always felt comfortable in front of goal."

Those goals have, after a failure to win a trophy in England, led to two Bundesliga titles and a German Cup. But success with England remains elusive after a 2026 World Cup exit in the semifinals. Kane will be 35 by the time of the next Euros, in the UK and Ireland in 2028, and has a deal with Bayern until the following year. His form since joining Bayern suggests that he could get better still.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

This article was first published on October 22, 2026. It was updated on October 27 after Harry Kane won the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

entries.title: Will elections in Israel change its Iran approach?
entries.summary: As Israelis head to the polls, the country's conflict with Iran casts a long shadow over the ballot box. But any leadership changes in Israel may not be enough to shake up its grand strategy on Tehran.
entries.content:
Asia

Will elections in Israel change its Iran approach?

October 27, 2026

As Israelis head to the polls, the country's conflict with Iran casts a long shadow over the ballot box. But any leadership changes in Israel may not be enough to shake up its grand strategy on Tehran.

Israel's vote this Tuesday is the first general election for the country since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023 — an assault which led to one of the deepest security crises in Israel's history.

As incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fights to retain power, the question is not merely who will lead Israel's next government, but also how that government will navigate the region-wide security crisis that was triggered by the attack and the Israeli reaction, which included launching a war against Iran.

US President Donald Trump recently issued a full-throated endorsement of the incumbent Israeli leader as a "warrior prime minister" and warned that any other choice would affect Israel's alliance with Washington.

"If Israel has the wrong leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi (Benjamin Netanyahu), America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump said in an online post, referring to the Iran conflict.

Behind the scenes, however, media reports indicated a rift between the Israeli government and the Trump administration. According to The Financial Times, the Israeli military intended to launch a new round of attacks on Iran's nuclear facilities, government centers, and energy infrastructure around October 10. However, Trump opposed the new escalation before the US midterm elections on November 3.

The Jerusalem Post later questioned the narrative, reporting that the army had no specific directive for such an operation.

Israel's moves hinge on Trump's decision

The Israeli race has turned into a tight duel between Netanyahu and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot — former IDF (Israel Defense Forces) chief of staff and leader of the front-running centrist party "Yashar."

But Raz Zimmt, the head of the Iran program at the Tel Aviv-based Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), warns political divisions between the two options are not deep enough to speak of a "fundamental change in Tel Aviv's approach toward Tehran" after the election.

"In the perception of Israel's left, right, and center factions regarding the Iranian threat, especially its nuclear threat, there are minor differences," Zimmt told DW.

Moreover, according to Zimmt, any military escalation against Iran depends "on the decision of the US president" far more than on the identity of Israel's prime minister.

"Overall, I do not expect Israel's policy toward Iran and its proxies to undergo dramatic changes, regardless of the future government's composition," he said.

INSS senior fellow Danny Citrinovitch agreed that one should not expect "fundamental changes" in Israel's Iran policy depending on the election outcome.

"Even if Netanyahu personally steps down from power, his influence and the policies shaped over recent years will not simply vanish," Citrinovitch told DW.

Hamas attack as a turning point for Israel and Iran

The current consensus on Iran can be traced to the Hamas terror attack three years ago. Before the assault, according to Navid Toobian from the US-based Middle East Media Research Institute, many believed Israel should deal with the Islamic Republic "in a limited and managed way" and confront only the arms of the so-called "Axis of Resistance." But October 7 completely changed the rules of the game.

While Israel had been aware of Iran's slogans calling for its destruction, it was believed that such calls had an "internal aspect" to rally the base of hardcore Islamists in Iran, Toobian said.

The terror strike by the Iran-allied Hamas, however, showed that Tehran "spares no effort to strike Israel."

What are US and Israel hoping to achieve in the Iran war?

Damon Golriz, a researcher at the Hague Institute for Geopolitics, also points to October 7 as the trigger of the "largest historical trauma of the Jewish nation."

"Preserving Iran's nuclear ambitions and continuous threats against Israel has intensified this fear that for a large portion of Israeli society, today's rulers in Iran have become a symbol of a historical threat," he told DW.

With that in mind, the current US and Israeli policy towards Iran follows three vectors, according to Golriz.

"First, the removal of the regime's leaders; second, industrial and infrastructural collapse," and third, orchestrating a civil war and what he called "geographic scissors" to dismember Iran with the help of armed Kurdish and Baluch separatists, he said.

The US and Israel, however, are not the only players in the conflict. In a recent report, the Reuters news agency cited senior Iranian security officials as saying that Tehran has prepared detailed operational plans for retaliatory strikes. Tehran warned that their retaliatory tools include destroying undersea fiber-optic communication cables in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, alongside targeting US-dependent data centers and AI infrastructure in the region.

Diplomacy: A missed opportunity?

Commenting on possible alternatives to military escalation, Golriz highlights a diplomatic opportunity that opened six months ago in Islamabad, when Tehran agreed to never initiate war or military operations against Israel.

"For the first time in the history of the Islamic Republic, the fundamental national security interests of Israel were signed by the presidents of Iran and the United States," according to Gorliz.

The first article of the Islamabad framework could have been "the beginning of the end for 'Death to America' slogans and anti-Jewish threats, including 'Death to Israel," Golriz said.

This diplomatic window was quickly closed, but "with political will, the provisions and spirit of the Islamabad Memorandum will be the first strategic step toward lasting peace," he said.

But INSS senior fellow Citrinovitch was less optimistic when assessing the willingness of Israeli elites to return to diplomacy.

"Currently, returning to the nuclear deal has no place in Israel's political arena," he told DW.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Denmark's Frederiksen criticizes Finland and Norway for calling Putin without coordinating with allies, despite consultation with Ukraine
entries.summary: Finland and Norway have called Putin about ending the Ukraine war, drawing Danish criticism. The dispute highlights divisions over European engagement with Moscow ahead of planned US-led peace talks.
entries.content:
Norway

Denmark criticizes Finnish and Norwegian call with Putin on Ukraine

October 27, 2026

Finland and Norway have called Putin about ending the Ukraine war, drawing Danish criticism. The dispute highlights divisions over European engagement with Moscow ahead of planned US-led peace talks.

Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized Finland's and Norway's leaders Tuesday after they held a joint phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin about ending the war in Ukraine.

The call came ahead of planned US-led peace talks, which European leaders are seeking to join.

Why did Denmark criticize the call?

Frederiksen said that Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store had gone "solo.”

"I'm very sceptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative. It hasn't been coordinated with any of the rest of us," she told reporters while attending a meeting of Nordics leaders.

"I honestly don't know what those two countries think they can achieve with this."

"I believe we should keep Europe united, rather than going it alone," Frederiksen said.

Stubb and Store said they had consulted Ukraine before initiating the call.

They stressed that they represented their own countries and were not speaking on behalf of Europe.

What did the leaders discuss with Putin?

Stubb described the conversation as "frank and substantive." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed the call, the first between the three leaders.

"The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Stubb said.

Finland and Norway both border Russia and have supported Ukraine throughout the war.

Store said the leaders had emphasized de-escalation.

"The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations," he said.

How was Ukraine involved?

The call followed an October 20 meeting in Oslo involving Stubb, Store, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US envoy Steve Witkoff. US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner joined remotely.

Zelenskyy also spoke with the Nordic leaders after their conversation with Putin.

"Finland and Norway will continue to support Ukraine, and the efforts to find a just and lasting peace," Stubb wrote on social media.

A US-mediated ceasefire ‌in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky is set to last until November 1,

Ukraine's ‌top negotiator Davyd ‌Arakhamia said ‌on Tuesday.

"This is the biggest de-escalation since 2022," he said on Telegram, adding that every ‌such step brings peace closer.

entries.title: Jordan acknowledges civilian casualties in Syria airstrike against 'Islamic State'
entries.summary: A Jordanian government spokesman has expressed "regret" over civilian casualties in an airstrike it said was targeting "IS" militants.
entries.content:
October 27, 2026

A Jordanian government spokesman has expressed "regret" over civilian casualties in an airstrike it said was targeting "IS" militants.

The Jordanian government admitted on Tuesday that a number of civilians had been killed in airstrikes conducted against so-called "Islamic State" militants in southern Syria on Monday night.

The Jordanian air force carried out the strikes on "terrorist groups" in the region in retaliation for last week's attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox Church in Jordan in that killed nine people, adding the strikes killed more than 20 IS fighters.

However, Syrian authorities contradicted the claim, saying the strikes in the Daraa and Sweida provinces had killed seven people including three children and a woman. Two men who were killed were reportedly elderly.

One resident, Masoud al-Salim, said he lost his wife, son and three grandchildren in one of the strikes that hit his home in the Syrian border village of Al-Tuff.

"I came running and found there was no house anymore, no tent, nothing. I couldn't find anyone," he told the Associated Press, which said he was rummaging through children's schoolbooks and toys in the rubble.

"I started looking under the rubble. I thought they might be buried there."

Jordan admits civilians killed

On Tuesday, Jordanian Communications Minister ​Mohammed al-Momani acknowledged the civilian casualties, which he said the Hashemite Kingdom regretted.

"Jordan always takes all precautions to avoid harming civilians," he said in a post on social media, insisting: "The operations were carried out based on field intelligence to neutralize confirmed threats and terrorist operations against Jordan."

He said the Jordanian air force had inflicted "heavy losses in IS ranks, estimated at more than 20 elements" and destroyed a "massive weapons depot belonging to the organization."

"Jordan refrained from targeting sites where intelligence indicated the presence of civilians and regrets the occurrence of civilian casualties," he added.

Syria condemns 'violation'

Monday's operation sparked anger in Syria, where the Foreign Ministry condemned the strikes as an "unacceptable violation [of] and encroachment [into]" Syrian airspace.

While the Jordanian military claimed the strikes were conducted in coordination ⁠with Damascus, ​the Syrian government said they were carried ​out without prior coordination and announced an investigation.

Jordan and Syria maintained strong bilateral ties following the downfall of the Assad dynasty in December 2024 and the emergence of interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa's Islamist-led government.

Despite Monday's airstrike, Syria asserted that that both countries' leaderships will strengthen security coordination to "obstruct any efforts to destabilize the two countries' security and spill the blood of its people."

No group has claimed responsibility for the initial attack on the Greek Orthodox funeral in Jordan, but Jordanian security forces arrested three men – two brothers and their in-law – following a shootout earlier on Monday.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: DR Congo reports over 10,000 Ebola cases as the outbreak spreads abroad, with no approved vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo virus
entries.summary: DR Congo has reported more than 10,000 Ebola cases and nearly 4,900 deaths. The outbreak involves a virus for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment, complicating efforts to contain its spread.
entries.content:
October 27, 2026

DR Congo has reported more than 10,000 Ebola cases and nearly 4,900 deaths. The outbreak involves a virus for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment, complicating efforts to contain its spread.

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo reported that Ebola cases had risen to 10,060, with 4,887 deaths since the outbreak was identified in mid-May.

The outbreak involves the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has described it as the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

Where else have cases been reported?

Kenya has confirmed nine infections, including two deaths, after a patient traveled from DR Congo through Uganda to the capital, Nairobi.

Nigeria also confirmed an infection in a Swiss woman, the wife of a Swiss diplomat, who fell ill after visiting Uganda. Authorities are investigating where she contracted the virus. She was evacuated to Switzerland.

Why is the outbreak difficult to contain?

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person. It can cause fever, diarrhea and, in some cases, bleeding.

Early symptoms can resemble malaria, potentially delaying isolation and treatment.

The lack of an approved vaccine or specific treatment against the Bundibugyo virus further complicates efforts to control the outbreak.

Are vaccines and treatments being tested?

Clinical trials of two antiviral treatment approaches have been underway since July.

Two further trials are investigating whether the Ervebo vaccine can protect against the Bundibugyo virus. The vaccine is currently approved and recommended only against Ebola virus, formerly known as Zaire ebolavirus.

entries.title: Germany's Merz says erosion of global order means middle powers in Europe and Asia must be more assertive
entries.summary: During a visit to Singapore, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Europe and Germany want to increase free trade with open competition, reliability and a rules-based order.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Merz in Asia says middle powers must 'assert ' interests

Published October 27, 2026last updated October 27, 2026

During a visit to Singapore, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Europe and Germany want to increase free trade with open competition, reliability and a rules-based order.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • German Chancellor Merz is on a multi-day tour of Asia to promote new forms of cooperation and trade
  • Germany's defense minister calls for 'a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO'
  • Court rules to proceed with case against Nord Stream sabotage suspect

Keep reading for a roundup of what's making news in Germany on Tuesday, October 27, 2026:

Don't want to miss our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section 'Act with confidence' in Chinese market, Steinmeier tells German companies

'Act with confidence' in Chinese market, Steinmeier tells German companies

On the first day of his farewell tour in China, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier urged the German business community to act with confidence in the Chinese market.

"When you travel in China, you're amazed at how highly Germany and German technology are still valued here," he said in Hefei. "That's why we can act with confidence in these markets."

Steinmeier did not bring any companies with him to China as part of his delegation, as his final trip was intended to focus on culture and science.

Nevertheless, the first day of the trip in Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province, revolved primarily around the economy. Steinmeier visited the Volkswagen China Technology Company (VCTC). About three years ago, Europe's largest automaker opened a research center for electric mobility there, which today employs 3,000 people.

Johannes Volkmann, a lawmaker accompanying Steinmeier in China, warned that the German economy must not "lose its leadership in innovation."

"I'm taking this call to action with me from here to do more to improve competitive conditions at home," he said, adding that Germany must avoid creating new dependencies "by allowing innovation and value creation to take place only outside Europe."

Steinmeier called for Europe to reposition itself and reorganize its economic instruments with its growing trade deficit with China in mind. 

"The trade surplus that China is accumulating naturally causes us concern because the successful model of economic cooperation is becoming unbalanced," he said. "We must strive to ensure that economic cooperation does not come to an end, but that it continues — to the mutual benefit of both sides."

Germany's trade deficit with China amounted to just under €90 billion ($100 billion) in 2025. According to the Federal Statistical Office, China exported goods worth €170.6 billion to Germany, and German exports to China amounted to €81.3 billion.

Across the 27-member EU, the deficit amounted to almost €197 billion in the first half of 2026, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic.

Additional reporting by Rosalia Romaniec in Hefei.

Skip next section Court rejects bid to end case against Ukrainian over Nord Stream blasts

Court rejects bid to end case against Ukrainian over Nord Stream blasts

A German court denied a defense request to end the trial of a former Ukrainian army officer who stands accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines.

Serhii Kuznietsov, 50, went on trial this month at the Hamburg state court, charged with causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public services and being an "accomplice to war crimes" by attacking civilian infrastructure.

Prosecutors accuse him of being the ringleader of the destruction, considered one of Europe's biggest acts of post-World War II sabotage. He is alleged to have carried out the explosions together with six others.

His lawyers said the charges should be dismissed, arguing that, as a former soldier, Kuznietsov was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak for national security reasons and could face severe penalties in Ukraine if he did. They argued that, under German law, anyone who cannot speak on his or her own behalf cannot be convicted.

The Hamburg court ruled Kuznietsov's defense was not limited under German law and that freedom to testify is not limited by a foreign country's conditions of service.

The undersea explosions on September 26, 2022, damaged the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, which brought Russian natural gas to Germany until Moscow cut off supplies in August 2022.

The blasts also damaged the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never went into service. Germany suspended the pipeline's certification process shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Italian authorities detained Kuznietsov last year. He was publicly named in extradition proceedings that led to his transfer to Germany in November.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has denied allegations that his country was involved in the pipeline blasts.

Skip next section Mercedes cuts outlook for 2026 profit margin

Mercedes cuts outlook for 2026 profit margin

German carmaker Mercedes-Benz has cut its forecast for 2026, with difficult market conditions in China and higher fourth-quarter cost expectations set to negatively impact profits, the company said on Tuesday.

Markets were quick to take note of the announcement, and Mercedes shares dropped 3.4% in trading on Tuesday morning.

The move makes Mercedes the third big German carmaker to lower its outlook for 2026 after BMW and VW took similar steps.

Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Kaellenius has called on German employees to work more without pay while also expanding manufacturing operations in Hungary, where he said costs are about 70% lower than in Germany.

Mercedes currently expects an adjusted car profit margin of 2% to 3% in 2026, compared to the 3% to 5% in the previous guidance.

Like many German automakers, Mercedes has faced weak sales in China. German carmakers have struggled in the world's largest car market with sluggish demand and increased competition from local manufacturers.

Mercedes vehicle deliveries in China — last year already at their lowest level since 2016 — fell a further 29% in the nine months to the end of September.

Mercedes also released third-quarter figures earlier than planned, which showed that the company generated just €172 million ($191 million) in free cash flow from its vehicle business, down on the €422 million forecast by financial market experts.

Before interest and tax, Mercedes posted an operating profit of €1.77 billion — more than double the €750 million recorded a year earlier, according to the preliminary figures. But last year's stats were significantly impacted by one-time expenses, especially related to job cuts and legal disputes.

Adjusted for one-off items, the operating profit margin in the passenger car business stood at 2.5%, down on the 4.8% recorded a year earlier.

Skip next section Some 5% of Germany potentially suitable for long-term nuclear waste storage

Some 5% of Germany potentially suitable for long-term nuclear waste storage

The German agency responsible for finding a final repository for nuclear waste (BGE) has eliminated five states from its search.

Berlin, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony and Saarland were deemed unsuitable for long-term radioactive waste storage.

In a report issued Tuesday, the BGE said it had limited its search to 5% of Germany, down from 25% in 2025. The federal agency aims to suggest suitable locations for final evaluation by the end of 2027.

Regions in northern, northwestern, southern and eastern Germany remain under consideration as locations for final storage facilities.

Germany's nuclear waste is currently stored in 16 above-ground interim storage facilities.

The BGE assessments evaluate regions' geological conditions and their ability to safely contain highly radioactive material. Granite, salt, and clay are generally considered potentially suitable types of rock and areas with damaged or compromised subsurface conditions, places with mines or volcanos have been active, are not eligible as final disposal sites.

Germany needs to find a repository for approximately 27,000 cubic meters of highly radioactive nuclear waste generated over more than 60 years of nuclear power generation. The site is expected to ensure safety for 1 million years. The last German nuclear power plants were decommissioned in April 2023.

BGE said its goal remains finding the site that offers the highest level of safety for highly radioactive waste.

The agency's recommendations, however, are not legally binding and it will be up to German lawmakers to determine the final disposal site.

Skip next section NSU terrorist Beate Zschäpe to stay in prison until at least 2035

NSU terrorist Beate Zschäpe to stay in prison until at least 2035

Convicted right-wing terrorist Beate Zschäpe's request for early release from prison was denied with a court ruling that she would remain behind bars for at least nine more years.

Munich's Higher Regional Court on Tuesday set her minimum term at at least 24 years and refused to suspend the sentence to probation. By determining her guilt to be particularly severe, the court effectively ruled out her release after 15 years, which, including her time in pretrial detention, would have expired this year.

The Munich court said Zschäpe, currently 51, still had a good chance of leaving prison alive.

The decision is not yet legally binding, and the defense and the Federal Prosecutor's Office can appeal.

Zschäpe had been sentenced to life in prison in 2018 as an accomplice in the National Socialist Underground (NSU) murders that killed 10 people, mainly individuals with an immigrant background as well as a police officer.

The terror group went undetected for a decade. Zschäpe's fellow NSU members, Uwe Mundlos and Uwe Böhnhardt, injured several people with bomb attacks in Cologne and killed themselves to avoid arrest in 2011.

Under normal conditions, a convict who receives a life sentence in Germany can apply for parole after 15 years.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Harry Kane breaks Bayern and Bundesliga's Ballon d'Or drought

IN DEPTH: Harry Kane breaks Bayern and Bundesliga's Ballon d'Or drought

Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has won football's most prestigious individual prize, beating Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.

Skip next section Pistorius wants 'stronger Europe within a stronger NATO'

Pistorius wants 'stronger Europe within a stronger NATO'

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, along with his counterparts from France, Italy, Poland and the UK, authored an op-ed calling Russia "the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability."

In the article, published online and in Tuesday's Tagesspiegel newspaper, the defense ministers wrote they "share a deep conviction" that European countries need to do more to ensure their own security and aim to build "a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO."

The ministers, however, added that the United States would remain an "indispensable ally."

The pronouncement comes as many in Europe are wary of US President Donald Trump's commitment to the NATO military alliance.

The US leader has threatened to leave the group and to seize control of Greenland, a territory of fellow NATO member Denmark. US presidents have repeatedly called for European NATO members to contribute more to the alliance's military capabilities.

As US support for Ukraine also appears to waver, the five defense ministers reiterated their political, military and financial support for Kyiv as it fights of Russia's full-scale invasion.

Skip next section Merz: Collapse of global order threatens middle powers in Europe and Asia

Merz: Collapse of global order threatens middle powers in Europe and Asia

In Singapore, to start a four-day business-oriented trip that will also bring him to Japan and South Korea, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said it was up to European and Asian nations to find their spot amid a changing global order.

"We must assert our interests in an international environment shaped by renewed great-power rivalry," Merz said.

With a view to unpredictable tariffs imposed by the United States under President Donald Trump and trade restrictions from China, Merz emphasized the stability offered by Germany and the rest of Europe.

"This is a deliberate counterpoint to what we are currently seeing. We want to do things differently, and we want to show that there is a better way," Merz said, adding that Europe sought to expand partnerships to increase free trade with open competition, reliability and a rules-based order.

He also called for increased international investment and cooperation.

"Under the federal government I lead, investment opportunities will be continuously improved," Merz said following a meeting with Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong. "I encounter a great deal of confidence here in Germany and in Europe as locations for investment."

The German leader called for a new free-trade agreement between the 27-member European Union and the Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), comprising 12 countries across five continents, including Australia, Canada, Japan, Mexico and the United Kingdom. Neither the United States nor China is part of the CPTPP.

For his part, Wong said investment in Germany and Europe would continue.

"Many of our investors, including our sovereign wealth funds, have been investing in Germany for a long time," Wong said. "They will continue to invest because they are confident that, in the long term, Germany and Europe have potential."

Merz and Wong agreed their nations would work to expand cooperation in security and defense as well as trade, investment, sustainable energy and artificial intelligence.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen and welcome to our daily coverage of what's making news in Germany. 

While we follow the news here in Berlin and Bonn, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is in Singapore, speaking about international cooperation among middle-power countries in Europe and Asia amid a "renewed great-power rivalry."

Today, we're also expecting a decision on whether to proceed with a case against a Nord Stream sabotage suspect and a report on Germany's ongoing search for a nuclear waste storage facility.

Not to mention a car ramming last night near the northern German city of Hannover that has left several people with serious injuries, while the suspects are still on the run.

entries.title: Two men face UK national security charges following an incident near RAF Fairford, with police suspecting Iranian state involvement
entries.summary: British prosecutors have charged two men over an incident near RAF Fairford in September. Police suspect Iranian involvement in the case at a base used for US strikes on Iran.
entries.content:
October 27, 2026

British prosecutors have charged two men over an incident near RAF Fairford in September. Police suspect Iranian involvement in the case at a base used for US strikes on Iran.

British prosecutors said Tuesday that two men had been charged under the National Security Act in connection with a September incident near RAF Fairford, an airbase used by US forces to launch strikes on Iran.

US bombers were withdrawn from Fairford on security grounds shortly after the arrests immediately after the incident.

What have police said about the Fairford suspects?

The Crown Prosecution Service charged Mohmed A., 24, of London, with engaging in conduct likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service. Counterterrorism police chief Laurence Taylor said investigators believed the country involved was Iran.

Nouman E., 24, also of London, was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on August 22. Both men were due to appear in court later Tuesday.

Nouman E. was initially arrested near the Gloucestershire base on September 27 and rearrested on October 20.

A separate suspect, a 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national also arrested on October 20, was released without charge over the suspected intelligence offense. He remains on bail following an October 1 arrest on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Five other men also remain on police bail.

How did the Fairford investigation begin?

Armed police responded to reports of three suspicious vehicles near the base on September 27 and arrested five men. Scores of residents were evacuated as police and military bomb-disposal experts searched the area for explosives.

Police have said they consider Iranian state involvement "highly likely."

"We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state," said Laurence Taylor, head of UK counterterrorism policing.

He said police were working with MI5, Britain's domestic intelligence service, to counter the threat and urged the public to report concerns.

Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said it considers bases used to attack its territory legitimate targets.
